tools.name: netobserv_export_flows
tools.description: Exports NetObserv flow records as CSV with the same filters as list_flows. Use when the user needs downloadable flow data for audits or offline analysis.

columns.description: Optional comma-separated column names to include (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace,DstK8S_Namespace,Bytes). Omit to export all columns present in the result.

endTime.description: End of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Defaults to now.

filters.description:
NetObserv filter expression passed to the console plugin (plain text; the client URL-encodes it).

Syntax:
- key=value — exact match; key=a,b — OR multiple values for the same key
- key~pattern — regex / contains match; key!~pattern — NOT regex
- key!=value — not equal; key>number — numeric greater-or-equal (e.g. Bytes>1000)
- AND within a group: & (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace=default&Proto=6)
- OR between groups: | (e.g. SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b)

Prefer the dedicated "namespace" parameter for namespace scope when possible.
Use Kubernetes list tools (namespaces, pods, deployments, etc.) to discover filter values.

Common Kubernetes fields (Src/Dst prefixes mirror each other):
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type (e.g. Pod, Service, Node)
- SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName, SrcK8S_OwnerType, DstK8S_OwnerType (for Deployment, StatefulSet, etc.)
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone, K8S_ClusterName, UDN

Network & flow:
- SrcAddr, DstAddr (IPs), SrcPort, DstPort, Proto (IANA number, e.g. 6=TCP, 17=UDP)
- FlowDirection (0=Ingress, 1=Egress, 2=Inner), Bytes, Packets, Dscp, Flags

Packet drops (often with recordType flowLog and packetLoss dropped/hasDrops):
- PktDropPackets, PktDropBytes, PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsId, DnsLatencyMs, DnsErrno, DnsFlagsResponseCode

Examples:
- SrcK8S_Namespace=openshift-netobserv&SrcK8S_Name~my-app
- Proto=6&DstPort=443
- SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b

format.description: Export format. Only csv is supported.

limit.description: Maximum number of flow records to return. Default 100.

namespace.description: Restrict results to flows where source or destination namespace matches (dev-scoped Loki tenant).

startTime.description: Start of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Overrides timeRange when set.

timeRange.description: Lookback window in seconds when startTime is omitted. Default 300.

tools.name: netobserv_get_flow_metrics
tools.description: Returns aggregated NetObserv flow metrics as topology or time-series data. Use for throughput, TLS/DNS/drop breakdowns, and namespace or workload traffic analysis; see aggregateBy and groups for grouping options.

aggregateBy.description:
Primary dimension for netobserv_get_flow_metrics (console plugin /api/flow/metrics).

Two forms (use exact spelling):

1) Topology scopes — aggregate endpoints for graph/topology views:
- app — application workloads (pods/services), excluding infrastructure traffic
- namespace — Kubernetes namespace (default)
- owner — controller owner (Deployment, StatefulSet, …)
- resource — pod, service, or node (finest workload granularity)
- host — node name
- zone — availability zone
- cluster — cluster name (multi-cluster)
- network — user-defined / secondary network name

2) Flow record fields — group by a single flow attribute (PascalCase field name).
Use for breakdown charts (TLS, DNS, drops, protocol). Field names match filters / flow logs.

TLS (requires TLS tracking on the FlowCollector):
- TLSVersion, TLSCipherSuite, TLSGroup, TLSTypes

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsFlagsResponseCode, DnsErrno

Packet drops:
- PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

Network / K8s (single-sided breakdown; pair with filters for src/dst):
- Proto, SrcPort, DstPort, FlowDirection, Dscp
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type, SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone
- K8S_ClusterName, SrcK8S_NetworkName, DstK8S_NetworkName

Pair aggregateBy with type and function:
- Throughput: type=Bytes or Packets, function=rate
- Flow count: type=Flows, function=count or rate
- DNS volume: type=DnsFlows, function=count
- DNS latency: type=DnsLatencyMs, function=avg, p90, or max
- RTT: type=TimeFlowRttNs, function=avg, min, or p90
- Drops: type=PktDropPackets or PktDropBytes, function=rate

Examples:
- aggregateBy=namespace, type=Bytes, function=rate
- aggregateBy=TLSVersion, type=Bytes, function=rate, filters=TLSTypes!~""
- aggregateBy=TLSGroup, type=Flows, function=count
- aggregateBy=DnsFlagsResponseCode, type=DnsFlows, function=count
- aggregateBy=PktDropLatestState, type=PktDropPackets, function=rate, packetLoss=dropped
- aggregateBy=resource, type=Bytes, function=rate, namespace=netobserv

- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matching stable)
  - Security configuration: same as stable (no specific securityContext beyond default)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed version constraint) so it targets both deployments
  - Port: 80, targetPort: 8080 (unchanged)

Result:
- engine-v2-1 is available with 2/2 ready pods.
- Service Endpoints now include 4 pods (2 from engine-v2-0 and 2 from engine-v2-1), so traffic is split ~50/50 across stable and canary.

Notes and quick checks:
- Kubernetes Services don’t support weighted distribution natively; the 50% split is achieved by equal pod counts.
- Verified Endpoints show 4 addresses for the Service on port 8080 (2 stable + 2 canary).

If you want to:
- Shift more traffic to canary: scale engine-v2-1 up or engine-v2-0 down to change the ratio.
- Roll back canary: either scale engine-v2-1 to 0 or set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- Fully promote canary: update the Service selector to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.1 and (optionally) scale down/remove engine-v2-0.

- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)

  - Container port: 80 (matching stable)
  - Security configuration: same as stable (no specific securityContext beyond default)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed version constraint) so it targets both deployments
  - Port: 80, targetPort: 8080 (unchanged)

Result:
- engine-v2-1 is available with 2/2 ready pods.
- Service Endpoints now include 4 pods (2 from engine-v2-0 and 2 from engine-v2-1), so traffic is split ~50/50 across stable and canary.

Notes and quick checks:
- Kubernetes Services don’t support weighted distribution natively; the 50% split is achieved by equal pod counts.
- Verified Endpoints show 4 addresses for the Service on port 8080 (2 stable + 2 canary).

If you want to:
- Shift more traffic to canary: scale engine-v2-1 up or engine-v2-0 down to change the ratio.
- Roll back canary: either scale engine-v2-1 to 0 or set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- Fully promote canary: update the Service selector to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.1 and (optionally) scale down/remove engine-v2-0.

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The Deployment’s container overrode the entrypoint with: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"] and args: ["nonexistent_command"], which caused CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Replaced the Deployment to remove the invalid command/args so the image’s default entrypoint runs.
- Kept image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and exposed containerPort: 8080 (the unprivileged image listens on 8080).
- imagePullPolicy set to IfNotPresent to avoid unnecessary pulls.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: app-6df8647c78-8pxf2 — 1/1 Running, 0 restarts, in namespace crashloop-test.

Want me to also create a Service to expose it (ClusterIP/NodePort) or add readiness/liveness probes?

  replicas: 1

    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx

          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources: {}
      restartPolicy: Always
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      schedulerName: default-scheduler

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The Deployment’s container overrode the entrypoint with: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"] and args: ["nonexistent_command"], which caused CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Replaced the Deployment to remove the invalid command/args so the image’s default entrypoint runs.
- Kept image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and exposed containerPort: 8080 (the unprivileged image listens on 8080).
- imagePullPolicy set to IfNotPresent to avoid unnecessary pulls.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: app-6df8647c78-8pxf2 — 1/1 Running, 0 restarts, in namespace crashloop-test.

Want me to also create a Service to expose it (ClusterIP/NodePort) or add readiness/liveness probes?

results.taskOutput:
I found the issue: the Deployment was using an invalid container image tag:
- image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag
This caused ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff.

Fix applied:
- Updated the Deployment debug/app to use a valid image:
  docker.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable

Result:
- Rollout created a new ReplicaSet and replaced the failing pod.
- Current status: Deployment Available=True, Ready 1/1.
- Running pod: app-cff87698-rhszf (1/1 Ready).
- Events confirm the new image pulled and started successfully.

If you prefer a different image registry or a pinned version tag (e.g., nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.27.2), tell me and I’ll update it. You can verify with:
- kubectl -n debug rollout status deploy/app
- kubectl -n debug get pods -o wide

I found the issue: the Deployment was using an invalid container image tag:
- image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag
This caused ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff.

Fix applied:
- Updated the Deployment debug/app to use a valid image:
  docker.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable

Result:
- Rollout created a new ReplicaSet and replaced the failing pod.
- Current status: Deployment Available=True, Ready 1/1.
- Running pod: app-cff87698-rhszf (1/1 Ready).
- Events confirm the new image pulled and started successfully.

If you prefer a different image registry or a pinned version tag (e.g., nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.27.2), tell me and I’ll update it. You can verify with:
- kubectl -n debug rollout status deploy/app
- kubectl -n debug get pods -o wide

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

What was wrong:
- homepage-pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the claim couldn’t bind.

What I changed:
- Created a StorageClass named "sc" using the local-path provisioner (rancher.io/local-path) with WaitForFirstConsumer.

Result:
- PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound (1Gi, RWO).
- Pod homepage-pod is Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane (podIP 10.244.0.31).

Optional follow-ups:
- If you’d rather not keep a separate “sc” class, we can recreate the PVC to use the existing “standard” StorageClass instead.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

Fixed.

What was wrong:
- homepage-pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the claim couldn’t bind.

What I changed:
- Created a StorageClass named "sc" using the local-path provisioner (rancher.io/local-path) with WaitForFirstConsumer.

Result:
- PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound (1Gi, RWO).
- Pod homepage-pod is Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane (podIP 10.244.0.31).

Optional follow-ups:
- If you’d rather not keep a separate “sc” class, we can recreate the PVC to use the existing “standard” StorageClass instead.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What was wrong:
- homepage-pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the claim couldn’t bind.

What I changed:
- Created a StorageClass named "sc" using the local-path provisioner (rancher.io/local-path) with WaitForFirstConsumer.

Result:
- PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound (1Gi, RWO).
- Pod homepage-pod is Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane (podIP 10.244.0.31).

Optional follow-ups:
- If you’d rather not keep a separate “sc” class, we can recreate the PVC to use the existing “standard” StorageClass instead.

results.taskOutput:
Found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking port 80 and non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready). This caused the pod to fail probes and never become Ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to:
  - Probe HTTP path / on port 8080 for both readiness and liveness.
  - Expose containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still listens on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-5b6b5f969f-fqgqt).
- Service: orders/webapp (ClusterIP 10.96.89.72:80 -> pod:8080).
- Verified from inside the pod that http://127.0.0.1:8080/ returns 200 OK.

How to access it
- From within the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your machine (temporary): kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

If you want external access via an Ingress, tell me the hostname you’d like to use and I can set it up.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

Found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking port 80 and non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready). This caused the pod to fail probes and never become Ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to:
  - Probe HTTP path / on port 8080 for both readiness and liveness.
  - Expose containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still listens on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-5b6b5f969f-fqgqt).
- Service: orders/webapp (ClusterIP 10.96.89.72:80 -> pod:8080).
- Verified from inside the pod that http://127.0.0.1:8080/ returns 200 OK.

How to access it
- From within the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your machine (temporary): kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

If you want external access via an Ingress, tell me the hostname you’d like to use and I can set it up.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: webapp
          image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
  labels:
    app: webapp
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: webapp
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

outputSteps.content:
Found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but the Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking port 80 and non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready). This caused the pod to fail probes and never become Ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to:
  - Probe HTTP path / on port 8080 for both readiness and liveness.
  - Expose containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still listens on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-5b6b5f969f-fqgqt).
- Service: orders/webapp (ClusterIP 10.96.89.72:80 -> pod:8080).
- Verified from inside the pod that http://127.0.0.1:8080/ returns 200 OK.

How to access it
- From within the cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From your machine (temporary): kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

If you want external access via an Ingress, tell me the hostname you’d like to use and I can set it up.

Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant any permissions on core API group pods (apiGroup ""), so pod-reader could not list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pod read permissions:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - Kept the existing rule allowing list on apps/deployments.

How to verify
- Check authorization:
  - kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- List pods using impersonation:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. Listing pods cluster-wide or in other namespaces will still be denied unless granted separately.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant any permissions on core API group pods (apiGroup ""), so pod-reader could not list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pod read permissions:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - Kept the existing rule allowing list on apps/deployments.

How to verify
- Check authorization:
  - kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- List pods using impersonation:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. Listing pods cluster-wide or in other namespaces will still be denied unless granted separately.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant any permissions on core API group pods (apiGroup ""), so pod-reader could not list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pod read permissions:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - Kept the existing rule allowing list on apps/deployments.

How to verify
- Check authorization:
  - kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- List pods using impersonation:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. Listing pods cluster-wide or in other namespaces will still be denied unless granted separately.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Nginx Deployment/pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: no endpoints -> Service wasn’t routing to any pod
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail since the container serves on 8080.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - Selector: app=nginx (to match the Deployment’s pods)
  - Port: name=http, port=80, targetPort=8080 (to match the container’s listening port)

Verification
- Endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.35:8080
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080
- The nginx pod is Running and Ready 1/1

How to test (inside the cluster)
- From any pod in the web namespace:
  - curl http://nginx
- From any namespace:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local

Note on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (internal only). If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on a node port
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it
  - Ingress: via your ingress controller (e.g., ingress-nginx)

Tell me which exposure method you prefer, and I can create the resource for you.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Nginx Deployment/pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: no endpoints -> Service wasn’t routing to any pod
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail since the container serves on 8080.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - Selector: app=nginx (to match the Deployment’s pods)
  - Port: name=http, port=80, targetPort=8080 (to match the container’s listening port)

Verification
- Endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.35:8080
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080
- The nginx pod is Running and Ready 1/1

How to test (inside the cluster)
- From any pod in the web namespace:
  - curl http://nginx
- From any namespace:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local

Note on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (internal only). If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on a node port
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it
  - Ingress: via your ingress controller (e.g., ingress-nginx)

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Nginx Deployment/pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: no endpoints -> Service wasn’t routing to any pod
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80.
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail since the container serves on 8080.

What I changed (fixed)
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - Selector: app=nginx (to match the Deployment’s pods)
  - Port: name=http, port=80, targetPort=8080 (to match the container’s listening port)

Verification
- Endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.35:8080
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080
- The nginx pod is Running and Ready 1/1

How to test (inside the cluster)
- From any pod in the web namespace:
  - curl http://nginx
- From any namespace:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local

Note on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (internal only). If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on a node port
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it
  - Ingress: via your ingress controller (e.g., ingress-nginx)

Tell me which exposure method you prefer, and I can create the resource for you.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed:

What was wrong
- Your Deployment (web-app-deployment) had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
- The cluster only has a single node without that label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. Events showed: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- With no pods behind the Service (web-app-service), connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the blocking nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Re-applied the Deployment.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-g5xns — 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-clwjp — 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints are now populated:
  - 10.244.0.37:80
  - 10.244.0.38:80
- The Service selector (app=web-app) matches the pod labels, so traffic should route correctly. The connection refused errors should stop.

If you actually need to pin this workload to special nodes
- Either restore the nodeSelector and label the intended nodes accordingly (kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or use node affinity with proper labels.
- On single-node/dev clusters, avoid restrictive nodeSelectors unless the node is labeled to match.

Optional hardening (recommended)
- Add readinessProbe to avoid sending traffic before the container is ready (for nginx, an HTTP GET on / port 80 works well).
- Consider resource requests/limits to improve scheduling behavior.

Let me know if you want me to add a readiness probe or reintroduce an appropriate affinity/selector with the matching node labels.

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Here’s what I found and what I fixed:

What was wrong
- Your Deployment (web-app-deployment) had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
- The cluster only has a single node without that label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. Events showed: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- With no pods behind the Service (web-app-service), connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the blocking nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Re-applied the Deployment.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-g5xns — 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-clwjp — 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints are now populated:
  - 10.244.0.37:80
  - 10.244.0.38:80
- The Service selector (app=web-app) matches the pod labels, so traffic should route correctly. The connection refused errors should stop.

If you actually need to pin this workload to special nodes
- Either restore the nodeSelector and label the intended nodes accordingly (kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or use node affinity with proper labels.
- On single-node/dev clusters, avoid restrictive nodeSelectors unless the node is labeled to match.

Optional hardening (recommended)
- Add readinessProbe to avoid sending traffic before the container is ready (for nginx, an HTTP GET on / port 80 works well).
- Consider resource requests/limits to improve scheduling behavior.

Let me know if you want me to add a readiness probe or reintroduce an appropriate affinity/selector with the matching node labels.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed:

What was wrong
- Your Deployment (web-app-deployment) had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
- The cluster only has a single node without that label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. Events showed: “didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- With no pods behind the Service (web-app-service), connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local resulted in connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the blocking nodeSelector from the web-app-deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Re-applied the Deployment.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-g5xns — 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-clwjp — 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints are now populated:
  - 10.244.0.37:80
  - 10.244.0.38:80
- The Service selector (app=web-app) matches the pod labels, so traffic should route correctly. The connection refused errors should stop.

If you actually need to pin this workload to special nodes
- Either restore the nodeSelector and label the intended nodes accordingly (kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or use node affinity with proper labels.
- On single-node/dev clusters, avoid restrictive nodeSelectors unless the node is labeled to match.

Optional hardening (recommended)
- Add readinessProbe to avoid sending traffic before the container is ready (for nginx, an HTTP GET on / port 80 works well).
- Consider resource requests/limits to improve scheduling behavior.

Let me know if you want me to add a readiness probe or reintroduce an appropriate affinity/selector with the matching node labels.

results.taskOutput:
I’ve set up the cluster per your requirements. Here’s what’s in place and how it enforces least privilege and isolation:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to distinguish environments (dev/shared/staging/prod)

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding namespace-admin in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
    - Subjects: corresponding User (alice/bob/charlie) + ServiceAccount (alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa)
    - roleRef: ClusterRole admin (scoped to the namespace)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding developers-view in dev-shared
    - Subjects: users alice, bob, charlie and SAs alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
    - roleRef: ClusterRole view
- No developer access was granted to staging or prod (so only cluster-admins can access)

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - requests.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - requests.cpu: 4
  - requests.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging and prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - requests.cpu: 8
  - requests.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces:
  - Applied in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - allow-same-namespace-ingress (pods can reach each other within same namespace)
  - allow-egress-same-namespace (egress within same namespace)
  - allow-egress-dev-shared (egress allowed to namespace dev-shared)
  - allow-dns (egress UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns in kube-system)
  - Effect: no cross-developer traffic; can only talk within own namespace and to dev-shared, plus DNS
- dev-shared:
  - np-default-deny (Ingress+Egress)
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces (from namespaces dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie + same-namespace)
  - allow-egress-same-namespace
  - allow-dns (egress UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns)
  - Effect: shared services are reachable from dev namespaces, but dev-shared does not initiate to dev namespaces
- staging and prod:
  - np-default-deny (Ingress+Egress)
  - allow-same-namespace-ingress and allow-egress-same-namespace
  - allow-dns (egress UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns)
  - Effect: completely isolated from all dev namespaces; only same-namespace traffic + DNS allowed

How this meets your requirements
- Separate namespaces created for each developer + shared/staging/prod
- RBAC gives each dev and their SA full control over only their namespace; read-only to dev-shared; no dev access to staging/prod
- Resource quotas applied per namespace with requested limits
- Network policies enforce:
  - Cross-developer isolation
  - Only own namespace and dev-shared are reachable from dev namespaces
  - Staging/prod isolated from dev
  - DNS access allowed everywhere
- Default deny policies are in place across all non-system namespaces

Notes and optional hardening
- “System services” beyond DNS: If your workloads need to call the Kubernetes API (kubernetes.default.svc) or other platform services in default/openshift-* namespaces, we can add narrowly-scoped additional egress allowances. The exact peers vary by cluster; it’s best to open only what’s required.
- If you want “full access” without allowing RBAC edits, we can replace admin with a tighter Role (e.g., edit + specific rules) in each dev namespace.
- LimitRange defaults (optional) can enforce per-pod/container default requests/limits to work well with the quotas.

If you’d like, I can export a single multi-document YAML bundle of all applied resources for version control, or add optional allowances for specific system services your apps require.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

I’ve set up the cluster per your requirements. Here’s what’s in place and how it enforces least privilege and isolation:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to distinguish environments (dev/shared/staging/prod)

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding namespace-admin in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
    - Subjects: corresponding User (alice/bob/charlie) + ServiceAccount (alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa)
    - roleRef: ClusterRole admin (scoped to the namespace)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding developers-view in dev-shared
    - Subjects: users alice, bob, charlie and SAs alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
    - roleRef: ClusterRole view
- No developer access was granted to staging or prod (so only cluster-admins can access)

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - requests.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - requests.cpu: 4
  - requests.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging and prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - requests.cpu: 8
  - requests.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces:
  - Applied in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - allow-same-namespace-ingress (pods can reach each other within same namespace)
  - allow-egress-same-namespace (egress within same namespace)
  - allow-egress-dev-shared (egress allowed to namespace dev-shared)
  - allow-dns (egress UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns in kube-system)
  - Effect: no cross-developer traffic; can only talk within own namespace and to dev-shared, plus DNS
- dev-shared:
  - np-default-deny (Ingress+Egress)
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces (from namespaces dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie + same-namespace)
  - allow-egress-same-namespace
  - allow-dns (egress UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns)
  - Effect: shared services are reachable from dev namespaces, but dev-shared does not initiate to dev namespaces
- staging and prod:
  - np-default-deny (Ingress+Egress)
  - allow-same-namespace-ingress and allow-egress-same-namespace
  - allow-dns (egress UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns)
  - Effect: completely isolated from all dev namespaces; only same-namespace traffic + DNS allowed

How this meets your requirements
- Separate namespaces created for each developer + shared/staging/prod
- RBAC gives each dev and their SA full control over only their namespace; read-only to dev-shared; no dev access to staging/prod
- Resource quotas applied per namespace with requested limits
- Network policies enforce:
  - Cross-developer isolation
  - Only own namespace and dev-shared are reachable from dev namespaces
  - Staging/prod isolated from dev
  - DNS access allowed everywhere
- Default deny policies are in place across all non-system namespaces

Notes and optional hardening
- “System services” beyond DNS: If your workloads need to call the Kubernetes API (kubernetes.default.svc) or other platform services in default/openshift-* namespaces, we can add narrowly-scoped additional egress allowances. The exact peers vary by cluster; it’s best to open only what’s required.
- If you want “full access” without allowing RBAC edits, we can replace admin with a tighter Role (e.g., edit + specific rules) in each dev namespace.
- LimitRange defaults (optional) can enforce per-pod/container default requests/limits to work well with the quotas.

If you’d like, I can export a single multi-document YAML bundle of all applied resources for version control, or add optional allowances for specific system services your apps require.

outputSteps.content:
I’ve set up the cluster per your requirements. Here’s what’s in place and how it enforces least privilege and isolation:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to distinguish environments (dev/shared/staging/prod)

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding namespace-admin in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
    - Subjects: corresponding User (alice/bob/charlie) + ServiceAccount (alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa)
    - roleRef: ClusterRole admin (scoped to the namespace)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding developers-view in dev-shared
    - Subjects: users alice, bob, charlie and SAs alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
    - roleRef: ClusterRole view
- No developer access was granted to staging or prod (so only cluster-admins can access)

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - requests.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - requests.cpu: 4
  - requests.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging and prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - requests.cpu: 8
  - requests.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces:
  - Applied in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - allow-same-namespace-ingress (pods can reach each other within same namespace)
  - allow-egress-same-namespace (egress within same namespace)
  - allow-egress-dev-shared (egress allowed to namespace dev-shared)
  - allow-dns (egress UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns in kube-system)
  - Effect: no cross-developer traffic; can only talk within own namespace and to dev-shared, plus DNS
- dev-shared:
  - np-default-deny (Ingress+Egress)
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces (from namespaces dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie + same-namespace)
  - allow-egress-same-namespace
  - allow-dns (egress UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns)
  - Effect: shared services are reachable from dev namespaces, but dev-shared does not initiate to dev namespaces
- staging and prod:
  - np-default-deny (Ingress+Egress)
  - allow-same-namespace-ingress and allow-egress-same-namespace
  - allow-dns (egress UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns)
  - Effect: completely isolated from all dev namespaces; only same-namespace traffic + DNS allowed

How this meets your requirements
- Separate namespaces created for each developer + shared/staging/prod
- RBAC gives each dev and their SA full control over only their namespace; read-only to dev-shared; no dev access to staging/prod
- Resource quotas applied per namespace with requested limits
- Network policies enforce:
  - Cross-developer isolation
  - Only own namespace and dev-shared are reachable from dev namespaces
  - Staging/prod isolated from dev
  - DNS access allowed everywhere
- Default deny policies are in place across all non-system namespaces

Notes and optional hardening
- “System services” beyond DNS: If your workloads need to call the Kubernetes API (kubernetes.default.svc) or other platform services in default/openshift-* namespaces, we can add narrowly-scoped additional egress allowances. The exact peers vary by cluster; it’s best to open only what’s required.
- If you want “full access” without allowing RBAC edits, we can replace admin with a tighter Role (e.g., edit + specific rules) in each dev namespace.
- LimitRange defaults (optional) can enforce per-pod/container default requests/limits to work well with the quotas.

If you’d like, I can export a single multi-document YAML bundle of all applied resources for version control, or add optional allowances for specific system services your apps require.
